Set up & run

Running many goals: orchestrate

Turn a batch of issues into a dependency graph and run it as parallel waves of goals, each in its own session.

On this page
  • Starting a batch
  • The dry run and the go-ahead
  • How many goals run at once
  • What is held
  • Follow-ups
  • When something fails
  • Reading progress
  • The other batch and planning skills

/sigma-orchestrate is for the day you have ten issues, not one. You give it a list, a GitHub search or a short description. It works out which goals must wait for which, groups the rest into waves that can run at the same time, and shows you one screen to approve. Then it starts one --land session per goal, watches them through GitHub, merges what the post-PR review approves and reports. It writes no product code itself.

Starting a batch

/sigma-orchestrate [--max-seats N] [--name BATCH] [--where cloud|local]
                   [--model auto|sonnet|opus] [--max-opus N]
                   [--no-merge] [--dry-run] [--yes]
                   <issue numbers | GitHub search | description>

The last part can be numbers (#12 34 56), a search such as is:open label:priority:P1 label:feature:x, or a description like "the open children of epic #N".

NeedsWhy
discovery.source: githubThe batch is read from, and tracked on, GitHub.
work.enabled onEach session must be allowed to land its own goal.
work.auto_merge of protected or alwaysOtherwise every session ends without a merge, the same way, so the batch stops up front.
Goals assigned to the GitHub account the sessions run asA goal assigned to someone else is not taken.
A way to start sessionsA host tool, or you start them from a printed list.

The dry run and the go-ahead

Everything up to the go-ahead only reads. You get one screen: the waves, what is held or needs you, how many sessions at once, where they run, the model mix, whether merging is on, a cost line from past goals (or "no data") and the follow-up rule.

--dry-run stops there and writes nothing to GitHub or the repository. Use it first. Without --yes you are asked before anything starts. A batch you stop is safe to resume: run it again with the same --name and it reads GitHub and continues.

How many goals run at once

SettingDefaultWhat it limits
--max-seats N (flag)no limit: every ready goal runs at onceMost goal sessions running at the same time.
parallel.goals.max_concurrent3With --where local and no --max-seats, this is the limit. One machine's memory and disk are the ceiling there.
--max-opus N (flag)no limitMost Opus sessions at once.
followups.max_added_slices10How many follow-ups one goal may add to its own plan as slices. A whole number of at least 1; anything else reads 10, never unlimited.

Width otherwise comes from the dependencies themselves: no two goals in a wave claim the same files, and a goal whose claims are unknown runs alone. Launches go out in groups of 10, pause on any rate-limit report, and each goal is launched at most twice.

What is held

  • A goal that has an open pull request on any branch.
  • A goal with an open blocker outside the batch, or part of a cycle.
  • Every goal that waits on a held goal.
  • Parked goals, closed goals, epics and other upper tiers are excluded, and each exclusion is told to you with its reason.

A held goal is not failed. It is listed in the report with the action that would free it.

Follow-ups

Work a goal finds along the way is decided by the project setting followups.mode, never by the launch prompt.

ValueBehaviour
in-goal (default)A find in the goal's own feature joins its plan as a slice. A separate goal is filed only for another feature, or once the goal holds followups.max_added_slices; the reason is recorded.
fileThe explicit opt-out for people: every find is filed as its own goal. Only the exact string file opts out; any other value reads in-goal.

When something fails

  • A session that parks keeps its own park; the batch reports it with the exact action for you.
  • A goal that fails is recorded as failed; goals that waited on it stay held. Nothing is merged on its behalf.
  • A pull request is merged only when its post-PR review approved the current head. An approval that names a different commit does not count.
  • Dependents are released after merges, but a parked goal is never resumed by the batch: that stays /sigma-unpark.

Reading progress

GitHub is the record: cloud sessions never report back, so the batch reads labels, pull requests, comments and commits. The batch carries the label orchestrate:<name>. A tracker file in the project's local state keeps the table of goals, and the final report lists merged, needs a person, held, and Opus use. See Cost and time for measured spend.

The other batch and planning skills

SkillUse it when
/sigma-orchestrateYou have many unrelated goals and want one session each, in waves, merged for you.
/sigma-chainYou want one end goal and everything it waits on solved in order, with all decisions asked up front.
/sigma-triageYou want a backlog drain planned and dependency-sequenced for a single /sigma-loop.
/sigma-dagYou want to see the stored dependency map: state, stuck and active chains, cycles.
/sigma-radarYou want current developments researched against the backlog as a ranked digest; it writes nothing external by default.
/sigma-prd-intakeYou have a product requirements file and want cited Dossiers plus one umbrella ticket.
/sigma-dossierYou have a business idea and want a Dossier from fixed questions, before any code is read.
/sigma-goal-designYou have a Dossier and want it mapped to code, blockers and slices in a design write-up.
/sigma-goal-reviewA design write-up needs independent confirmation before its slices are created.
/sigma-wizardFirst-run setup is incomplete and you want it guided one check at a time.

The full list is on Skills and commands. To run a batch in Claude Code's cloud, see Cloud sessions.

Not measured

No real batch has been run end to end with this skill. The wave planner, the follow-up setting and the head-naming approval are tested offline; the launchers, the merge checks and the wake loop have not been exercised on a live repository. A read-only validation of the first five steps found defects that were then fixed. The cost per merged goal is arithmetic from the code, not a measurement.

Technical detail

A wave is a set of goals where every in-batch blocker sits in an earlier wave and no two share a claim (a path, a glob cut back to the directory before its first wildcard, or an exact token; * means unknown and clashes with everything). Rank is priority, then how many in-batch goals wait on it, then issue number. Readiness is checked by ancestry: a blocker counts only once it has merged into the goal's own base, not merely when its issue is closed. A pull request awaiting merge holds its claims but no seat. The planner is standard-library code that makes no network call, so two check-ins over the same facts never disagree. Every GitHub read and write is REST, which works in cloud sessions. Sources: orchestrate, configuration, parallelism.
